Detect redundant pairs of items

Source: R/redundancy.R
redundancy.Rd

redundancy() detects pairs of items that measure nearly the same thing, which appear in a network as two nodes with nearly the same connections. Such topological overlap complicates the interpretation of the network, and of centrality in particular (Hallquist, Wright & Molenaar, 2021), so redundant pairs are commonly identified before a network is estimated, and then combined or reduced to one item.

The function compares, for every pair of items, their correlations with each of the other items, using a significance test for two dependent correlations that share a variable. A pair is flagged as redundant when the proportion of significantly different correlations is below threshold and the two items correlate above cor_min with each other. This is the procedure of goldbricker() in the networktools package.

It returns the flagged pairs, most redundant first.

To combine flagged items into one variable before estimating the network, net_aggregate() forms a composite score per group of items.

Usage

redundancy(
  data,
  p = 0.05,
  threshold = 0.25,
  cor_min = 0.5,
  cor_method = c("auto", "pearson", "spearman", "kendall")
)

# S3 method for class 'psychnet_redundancy'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A numeric data frame or matrix with one row per observation and one column per item.

p

Significance level of each test of two correlations. Default 0.05.

threshold

A pair is flagged when its proportion of significantly different correlations is below this value. Default 0.25.

cor_min

Minimum correlation between the two items: a pair is flagged only when its correlation exceeds this value. Default 0.5.

cor_method

Correlation type: "auto" (default; polychoric or polyserial correlations where items are ordinal, see cor_auto()), "pearson", "spearman" or "kendall".

x

A psychnet_redundancy object.

...

Unused.

Value

A data frame of class psychnet_redundancy, one row per flagged pair, most redundant first, with columns item1, item2, proportion (share of significantly different correlations) and correlation (the correlation of the two items); it has no rows when no pair is flagged. The proportions for all pairs are kept with the result as the attribute proportion_matrix. print() shows the flagged pairs, or a note that none were flagged, and returns x invisibly.

Details

Non-numeric columns are dropped, and so is any column that is constant once incomplete rows are removed. Rows with a missing value in any numeric column are dropped (listwise deletion, as in goldbricker()), and the number of remaining rows is the sample size of every test.

Functions

  • print(psychnet_redundancy): The thresholds used and the flagged pairs.

Conditions

psychnet_bad_input for an invalid argument, for data that are not a data frame or matrix, or for fewer than three usable items; psychnet_degenerate_sample when fewer than four complete rows remain; psychnet_rows_dropped (warning) when incomplete rows are dropped; psychnet_constant_variable (warning) when a constant column is dropped; psychnet_dropped_columns (a message) when non-numeric columns are dropped.

References

Hallquist, M. N., Wright, A. G. C., & Molenaar, P. C. M. (2021). Problems with centrality measures in psychopathology networks. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 56(2), 199-223.

See also

net_aggregate() to combine items; cor_auto() for the correlations.

Examples

redundancy(SRL_Claude)
#> # redundant pairs (proportion < 0.25, r > 0.50): 0 found
#>   none
